presenting_problem.situation: An elderly Caucasian man with a manual work background was referred for psychological assessment after repeated primary care visits centered on fears of an undetected serious illness, particularly cancer, despite unremarkable investigations and repeated medical reassurance.
impact: Repeated requests for medical reassurance from his primary care physician despite negative blood tests and scans.
Frequent checking of bodily sensations and monitoring for signs of illness throughout the day.
Extended time spent reading online cancer stories and symptom information.
Strain in the relationship with his physician, with appointments becoming tense and conflictual.
Reduced attention to routine responsibilities and social interactions because of persistent health-related preoccupation.

precipitating_factors: An increase in health anxiety followed repeated exposure to online accounts of people reportedly diagnosed with cancer after initially vague or missed symptoms.
Recent rounds of blood work and scans did not reduce help-seeking and appear to have intensified repeated checking and consultation.
The relationship with his physician has become strained, prompting referral after frequent return visits and ongoing distress.

psychological: Age 11: his father died suddenly of a heart attack, and the family often said afterward that he had 'ignored the signs' and might have lived if it had been caught earlier.
Across adult life in manual jobs, he learned to keep working through pain and only seek help when a problem was serious, making physical symptoms feel especially significant once noticed.
In his 60s, he spent months helping a coworker who was eventually diagnosed with advanced lung cancer after initially being told several tests were clear.
social: He came from a working-class environment in which men were expected to be stoic about stress but highly alert to physical breakdown that could stop them from working.
In later life he has had more unstructured time and easier internet access, increasing solitary health-related searching and repeated exposure to worst-case illness narratives.

internal: Normal bodily sensations or minor physical changes trigger focused monitoring; increased vigilance makes more sensations noticeable, which are then treated as evidence of serious illness.
Seeking reassurance from tests, appointments, or others brings short-term relief; when certainty does not last, anxiety returns and prompts more checking and reassurance-seeking.
Time spent searching for cancer information increases exposure to alarming examples, which heightens threat perception and reinforces catastrophic interpretation of vague symptoms.
external: Online health information and anecdotal cancer stories repeatedly reactivate fear after brief periods of reassurance.
Tense interactions with his physician leave him feeling dissatisfied after appointments, increasing the likelihood of further reassurance-seeking elsewhere.

internal: Wants help and is actively seeking a way to reduce the cycle of checking and reassurance-seeking.
Able to describe the sequence of symptoms, appointments, and triggers in a concrete way.
Remains motivated to obtain clarity and regain day-to-day functioning.
external: Has an established primary care connection and prior access to medical evaluation.
Ongoing contact with family members who have noticed the pattern and remain involved.
Likely familiar with routine, persistence, and practical problem-solving from years of manual work.

intermediate_beliefs: If I do not stay alert to every symptom, no one else will protect me in time.
If I need too much reassurance, people will get tired of me and back away.
I have to push to be taken seriously, because if I relax or trust others, I will be overlooked.
automatic_thoughts: They're missing something serious; by the time they find it, it'll be too late.
If I stop checking, I'll overlook the warning signs like my father did.
He's getting fed up with me too; people only stick around until I become a burden.
triggers: Noticing a new ache, bodily sensation, or normal age-related change, especially when alone and unoccupied.
Reading online stories about cancer being missed or hearing about someone whose serious illness was found late.
In therapy, feeling that his worries are being reframed too quickly, questioned, or not taken seriously enough.
coping_patterns: Repeatedly checks his body, tracks sensations across the day, and searches the internet for symptom and cancer information.
Seeks reassurance through extra calls, appointments, retelling symptoms, and asking others to comment on whether he looks unwell.
Alternates between clinging contact and abrupt withdrawal: he presses others for attention and certainty, then becomes terse, argumentative, or disengaged when he feels dismissed.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: Fear, apprehension, irritability, and frustration are readily accessible and often intense. Loneliness and grief are present but harder for him to stay with for long; they are quickly redirected into health-focused vigilance or conflict. Shame about needing reassurance is strong but poorly tolerated, so it tends to appear as defensiveness, skepticism, or complaint rather than direct acknowledgment. He has limited ease with vulnerable dependency and finds sustained comfort, sadness, and tenderness difficult to access openly.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants the therapist to take his fears seriously, offer steady guidance, and help him feel understood without dismissing him as a nuisance.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he repeats concerns or shows too much need, the therapist will become irritated, think he is wasting time, or pull back emotionally once he is seen as difficult.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He alternates between pressing for reassurance and detail, then becoming guarded, skeptical, or abruptly withdrawn when he senses distance or impatience; he may test the therapist's engagement by repeating health fears or missing parts of what was discussed.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants family to stay close, reassure him that he matters, and help him feel safe when he becomes frightened about his health.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he leans on them too much, they will become fed up, minimize his fears, or distance themselves while privately seeing him as needy.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He repeatedly brings up symptoms, seeks checking or reassurance, and then turns irritable or shuts down when relatives try to redirect him; afterward he may pull back from contact for a time while continuing to monitor whether they notice him.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants doctors to be thorough, persistent, and personally invested enough to make sure nothing serious is being missed.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that once initial tests are clear, clinicians will stop listening, rush him, and overlook a dangerous illness until it is too late.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He returns frequently for appointments, asks for repeated tests or explanations, closely monitors clinicians' tone for signs of dismissal, and becomes tense or argumentative when reassurance is not given in the exact form he wants.

situation: The patient is preoccupied with the conviction that a serious physical illness is being missed despite repeated medical reassurance and negative test results. The fear has narrowed into a persistent belief that cancer may be present and spreading undetected. Although blood work and scans have shown nothing, the patient feels certain something is wrong and suspects the doctor failed to catch it early enough. Much of the anxiety intensified after reading stories online about people who had only vague symptoms before receiving devastating diagnoses. The patient wants desperately to feel confident nothing is wrong yet cannot settle into reassurance, and even worries that the level of worry itself may be a symptom. The pattern has strained relationships; the patient's physician has become impatient enough that the patient feels medically unprotected. Overall, the patient appears trapped in a cycle of bodily vigilance, catastrophic interpretation, and repeated reassurance-seeking.

presenting_problem.situation: A school-age boy was brought for evaluation because a longstanding fear of crossing large bridges has become difficult to manage when travel routes cannot be avoided, particularly during required trips involving transportation for elderly family members.
impact: Marked distress beginning up to a week before anticipated bridge crossings.
Slow driving during bridge crossings with preference for the middle lane.
Use of multiple safety behaviors during crossings, including keeping the radio on, windows down, and a hard metal tool near the door.
Heightened distress at toll points and 'last exit' signs and increased scanning of bridge railings and escape routes.
Symptoms intensify in the presence of trucks, darkness, or bad weather.

precipitating_factors: Recent unavoidable trips involving bridge crossings to pick up elderly parents from the airport have increased the frequency and urgency of the problem.
Ongoing family caregiving demands have made route avoidance less workable, bringing the longstanding fear into sharper functional focus.

psychological: Around age 7 or 8: first memorable distress on a large bridge during a family car ride, after which he began watching the edges of bridges and asking how people would get out if a car crashed.
Through later childhood: developed a repeated pattern of bracing, watching railings, and tracking exits whenever riding across major bridges, suggesting an early-conditioned fear response.
For many years before presentation: limited bridge travel when possible, allowing the fear to remain untested and entrenched over time.
social: As a school-age child, transportation routes are determined by adults, limiting his sense of control when a bridge is part of the trip.
Family expectations around helping with necessary travel for older relatives may increase exposure to feared routes without reducing the underlying fear.

internal: Anticipatory worry begins days in advance, increasing physiological arousal and vigilance before the trip and making the eventual crossing feel more threatening.
When possible, route avoidance reduces distress in the short term, which reinforces continued fear of bridges and lowers opportunities for corrective experiences.

During crossings, safety behaviors such as driving slowly in the middle lane, keeping the radio on, windows down, carrying a metal tool, and scanning railings or exits provide temporary relief while maintaining attention on danger cues.
external: Large bridges on necessary travel routes create repeated high-stakes exposure in which avoidance is not always possible.
Conditions such as trucks, darkness, bad weather, toll areas, and 'last exit' signs increase arousal and reinforce the sense of danger around bridge travel.

internal: Recognizes that the feared outcome is unlikely despite intense distress.
Able to complete bridge crossings when unavoidable, indicating some retained functioning under stress.
Uses organized, deliberate strategies during crossings, suggesting capacity to learn structured coping skills.
external: Family responsibilities provide a concrete reason to engage in treatment and practice coping for necessary travel.
Access to adult caregivers who can participate in planning around transportation and appointments.

intermediate_beliefs: If I do not stay alert and prepared, bad things will happen and I will be trapped.
If I need too much help or reassurance, people might get tired of me or pull away.
I have to stay close to trusted adults and keep checking that they are there, or I could be left alone when something bad happens.
automatic_thoughts: We're stuck on this bridge and something bad could happen before we can get off.
If we miss the exit or get boxed in by trucks, there won't be any way out.
I have to stay extra careful or nobody will help in time.
triggers: Anticipating an upcoming trip that requires crossing a large bridge, especially in the days before travel.
Bridge-specific cues such as toll booths, last-exit signs, trucks nearby, darkness, bad weather, and seeing bridge railings or limited escape routes.
In therapy, discussing bridge crossings in detail or being asked to imagine or plan an exposure without clear reassurance and adult support.

During bridge crossings, goes very slowly and prefers the middle lane.
Keeps the radio on, windows down, a metal tool near the door, and closely watches railings, toll points, and last exits.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: He readily experiences fear, dread, and tense anticipation, especially before expected bridge travel. He can access concern for family members and brief relief after a crossing is over. He appears to have more difficulty tolerating uncertainty, helplessness, and separation-related vulnerability, and may have limited capacity to express sadness or need directly before it escalates into clingy reassurance-seeking or heightened fear.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants caregivers to keep him safe, stay emotionally close, and provide steady reassurance during stressful travel.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that adults may need him to go along with necessary trips even when he is very scared, and may not fully grasp how intense the fear feels to him.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He becomes more watchful, seeks repeated reassurance, stays physically close, and relies on adults while also using visible safety behaviors during travel.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants acceptance, protection from embarrassment, and reassurance that others will not reject him if he seems scared.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He may tentatively expect that if his fear looks unusual or excessive, other children could tease him, lose patience, or not understand.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He may avoid showing fear openly, stay quiet about the problem, or cling more to familiar companions in stressful situations.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants the therapist to feel safe, reliable, and consistently available, and to help him handle feared situations without being overwhelmed.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He may worry that if he shows too much fear, dependency, or repeated need for reassurance, the therapist will become frustrated, dismiss the problem, or stop being as warm and engaged.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He is likely to watch closely for signs of approval or disconnection, seek reassurance about how therapy will work, and become more tense or avoidant if he senses distance or pressure.

situation: The patient experiences severe anticipatory and in-the-moment anxiety about crossing large bridges, a fear that becomes especially intense when the route cannot be avoided, such as driving to pick up elderly parents from the airport. The distress begins a week in advance and builds steadily. During the crossing, the patient vividly imagines the car flying off the bridge, drives slowly in the middle lane, keeps the radio on and windows down, and even keeps a hard metal tool by the door to break the glass in an emergency. Anxiety peaks near toll points and 'last exit' signs and worsens with trucks, bad weather, or darkness. The patient knows the risk is objectively low but still scans railing spacing as if calculating escape routes. Overall, the patient seems caught between a strong sense of duty toward family and an entrenched bridge phobia present for many years.

presenting_problem.situation: A senior African American male college student with strong academic and extracurricular functioning was referred after experiencing a recent cluster of recurrent panic attacks, including nighttime episodes and one during a school break, in the context of heavy academic, athletic, and leadership demands as graduation approaches.
impact: Recurrent panic attacks over the past month, totaling approximately five to six episodes.
Episodes include shortness of breath, visible fear, and acute distress.
Several attacks have occurred at night, disrupting sleep.
At least one attack occurred during a school break, suggesting episodes are not limited to periods of immediate academic demand.
He has not disclosed the attacks to friends and is presenting for help after the episodes began recurring.

precipitating_factors: Over the past semester, pressure has intensified around graduation planning, a looming transition out of college, and decisions about next steps after school.
Recent leadership demands in athletics and other campus responsibilities have increased performance pressure and reduced recovery time.
A cluster of five to six panic attacks over the past month, including nighttime episodes and one during a break from academic demands, prompted referral for evaluation.

psychological: From early high school onward, he was known in his family as the one who could handle a full load without complaining, and he learned to keep strain to himself while meeting expectations.
Age 17: during the college recruitment process, he balanced academics and sports while minimizing stress in order to avoid appearing less capable to coaches and teachers.
Throughout college, he has repeatedly taken on overlapping high-responsibility roles and relied on pushing through fatigue rather than scaling back commitments.
social: As an African American male student in predominantly white academic and athletic spaces, he may have felt ongoing pressure to appear exceptionally competent, calm, and self-sufficient in order to avoid negative judgment.
Campus and family messaging that success requires endurance, leadership, and not falling behind may have reinforced overcommitment and reluctance to show vulnerability.

internal: Panic sensations lead him to monitor his breathing and body closely, which increases alarm and makes subsequent episodes more likely.
Keeping the attacks private reduces opportunities for reassurance and practical support, leaving him to manage symptoms alone and heightening anticipatory anxiety.
Trying to maintain high performance across school, sports, and leadership roles limits rest and recovery, increasing physiological arousal and sensitivity to panic symptoms.
external: Approaching graduation and multiple performance-based roles keep daily stress levels elevated with little unstructured downtime.
Campus expectations to appear composed, dependable, and high-achieving may discourage disclosure and delay support-seeking.

internal: Strong academic discipline and follow-through, demonstrated by sustaining a double major and good grades.
Accustomed to working within demanding schedules and team expectations, which may translate into treatment adherence.
Despite hesitation about medication, he is help-seeking now and appears motivated to understand the episodes.
external: Maintains close contact with family who value education and are likely to respond if informed of his symptoms.
Has structured ties to campus through athletics, academic advising, and student organizations that could support treatment attendance and monitoring.
Stable housing and continued enrollment provide access to student health and counseling services.

intermediate_beliefs: If I am really capable, I should be able to handle stress on my own without letting it show.
If I slow down, ask for help, or cannot perform consistently, people will see that I am not enough.
The safest way to stay respected is to stay in control, keep producing, and not burden other people with my problems.
automatic_thoughts: Something is wrong with me; I should be able to handle this.
If I lose control in front of people, they'll see I'm not as solid as they think.
I need to keep this to myself and push through it.
triggers: Periods of high cumulative demand tied to graduation, leadership responsibilities, athletic commitments, and uncertainty about next steps after college.
Internal bodily sensations such as shortness of breath, chest tightness, waking suddenly at night, or noticing changes in breathing during times of fatigue.
In therapy, being asked to slow down, discuss vulnerability, or consider depending on others before he feels trust and control in the relationship.
coping_patterns: He keeps panic episodes and distress private from friends, teammates, and peers and continues meeting obligations without disclosing symptoms.
He overprepares, stays busy, and maintains a full schedule across academics, athletics, and leadership roles rather than scaling back when overwhelmed.
He minimizes symptoms, gives brief factual accounts of distress, and redirects attention to performance, logistics, or problem-solving instead of asking for comfort.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: He more readily accesses determination, irritability, pressure, and brief flashes of fear than sustained sadness, helplessness, or dependency. Acute panic breaks through his usual self-control, but shame about needing help is difficult for him to tolerate or express. He is likely to appear composed while carrying high internal tension and may have limited comfort with openly showing vulnerability, uncertainty, or need.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants the therapist to be competent, respectful, and helpful without being intrusive, and to offer a way to regain control of his symptoms.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he reveals too much distress, the therapist may see him as less capable, focus too much on weakness, or push emotional disclosure before he is ready.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He presents as polite, controlled, and high-functioning; shares symptoms in a narrowed, factual way; tests the therapist's reliability before disclosing more; and may detach or become less forthcoming if he feels examined too quickly.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants family members to feel proud of him and to provide support without worrying excessively or questioning his strength.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he tells them how overwhelmed he feels, they may become alarmed, disappointed, or respond with messages about enduring and staying strong.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He downplays distress, offers reassurance that he is managing, and keeps contact focused on achievements, plans, and responsibilities rather than panic symptoms.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants friends and teammates to see him as dependable, steady, and respected while still feeling accepted as part of the group.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that visible anxiety or loss of composure could lead others to judge him, treat him differently, or lose confidence in his leadership.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He conceals episodes, avoids discussing fear, and works harder to appear calm, productive, and available even when physiologically overwhelmed.

situation: The patient is a senior college student who appears highly functional on the surface, juggling a double major, athletics, sorority responsibilities, and strong grades, yet has recently been unsettled by a series of panic attacks that feel frightening and unexplained. Over the past month, five or six attacks have occurred, many at night and at least one during a break with no academic pressure, which shook the assumption that the episodes were tied to ordinary stress. During the attacks the patient feels scared, short of breath, and helpless. Underneath the confusion are hints of cumulative pressure: approaching graduation, leadership expectations on a sports team, and the edge of a major life transition. The patient has not told friends about the attacks and feels wary of medication. Overall, the patient seems frightened less by a specific trigger than by the feeling that alarming symptoms are appearing from nowhere just as adult expectations are intensifying.

presenting_problem.situation: An adult male working freelance from home presented for assessment due to worsening anxiety in professional and interpersonal situations, particularly around older authority figures and people perceived as emotionally explosive. Although symptoms initially improved after leaving a highly conflictual workplace in early adulthood, he now reports anxiety generalizing to otherwise safe interactions and increasing difficulty imagining a return to in-person office work.
impact: Becomes visibly awkward and tense during interactions, particularly with older authority figures or emotionally intense people.
Jumbles words and struggles to speak smoothly in professional conversations when under scrutiny or anticipating conflict.
Avoids or limits in-person office settings and is increasingly reluctant to consider returning to workplace-based roles.
Shows anticipatory anxiety before meetings or contact in which someone might become upset or critical.
Experiences persistent bodily alarm responses even in interactions where no actual anger is present.

precipitating_factors: A recent dream in which a previously supportive work contact was yelling appears to have highlighted that the fear has spread beyond overtly explosive people to safe professional relationships.
Growing pressure to consider more in-person professional contact has made the possibility of returning to office environments feel increasingly unmanageable.
Recent episodes of becoming visibly tense and verbally disorganized even with kind people have made the problem harder to contain through simple avoidance.

psychological: Age 20: in an early workplace, he spent extended periods around chronically angry, emotionally explosive coworkers and senior staff, with conflict felt as a constant background condition.

demographics.name: Michael Turner
demographics.occupation: Unemployed office worker currently seeking administrative/office work

presenting_problem.situation: An adult Caucasian male office worker involved in active parenting was referred for treatment after increasing anxiety began to interfere with his job search. He has become more reluctant to attend interviews following repeated encounters in which interviewers or others commented on his appearance, family situation, or lifestyle in ways that appeared to question his need for work. Similar incidents in parenting and community settings have been followed by broader social withdrawal and escalating distress around evaluative situations.
impact: Marked anxiety and visible tension before scheduled job interviews.
Avoidance or delay in submitting applications or confirming interviews.
Sleep disruption the night before interviews or networking meetings.
Difficulty concentrating during interview preparation and other job-search tasks.
Reduced willingness to engage socially with other parents and unfamiliar people.

precipitating_factors: Over the past several months, repeated interview experiences included comments about his appearance, family situation, and lifestyle that questioned whether he genuinely needed employment.
Similar remarks in parent and community settings increased recently, reinforcing a pattern of being judged before being known.
As he continued applying for office-based work, anticipatory distress before interviews intensified and prompted help-seeking.

psychological: Age 11: after his father lost a job unexpectedly, family conversations became highly focused on appearing respectable and not giving others reasons to judge the household.

In his first long-term office role in his 20s, a supervisor repeatedly praised his polished presentation while overlooking his workload, creating a recurring link between visible appearance and others minimizing effort.

During early parenthood, he took on a large share of scheduling, school coordination, and household planning while receiving frequent comments from acquaintances that he 'didn't look stressed,' a pattern he recalls as increasingly hard to brush off.
social: He has spent years in office environments where presentation, marital status, and lifestyle cues are often read quickly as markers of reliability or financial need.

In his parenting and social circles, there has been recurring casual commentary that well-dressed, composed parents are 'lucky' or have it easy, leaving little room for the less visible labor of family management.

external: Interview settings and casual social encounters continue to contain ambiguous or intrusive comments, reinforcing expectation of being judged on surface cues.

external: Ongoing family responsibilities that provide daily structure and a clear reason to re-engage with employment.
Access to office-sector work history and practical familiarity with interview and job-search processes.

situation: The patient becomes intensely nervous whenever speaking or performing in front of others, and this fear seems organized around a humiliating memory from elementary school when the patient's voice cracked during a presentation, everyone laughed, and it felt like the worst possible public failure. Since then, standing in front of people has meant anticipating blanking out, being laughed at again, and proving to themselves that they are the one person who cannot do what everyone else manages. The anxiety is specific rather than generalized: the patient is fine in ordinary group situations but wants to run away once attention is focused on them. The pattern has led to years of avoidance, including going to the nurse's office instead of presenting. The immediate trigger for seeking help is an upcoming singing test, which feels especially threatening. Yet the patient is not completely resigned: another part wants a different outcome this time and keeps practicing even while feeling scared.

situation: The patient has been anxious since youth and is especially burdened by social worries that arise after communicating with other people, particularly through text messages and email, where the patient repeatedly replays whether what was written was appropriate, rude, or made the other person uncomfortable. This does not happen with parents or siblings, but with almost everyone else messages are mentally reviewed after the fact, not because dramatic consequences usually follow, but because the possibility of having created discomfort lingers as a guilty weight. The same pattern shows up face-to-face: when a friend's partner invited the patient fishing, the patient worried about asking too many beginner questions, then worried the conversation was not flowing, and feared stressing the other person despite genuinely wanting the time together to be pleasant. The patient connects some of this vigilance to being a sexual minority, becoming especially careful around certain people. Overall, the patient seems kind and deeply motivated not to burden others, yet so alert to possible disapproval that ordinary interaction becomes prolonged self-monitoring.

presenting_problem.situation: An adult Caucasian woman working in a program or administrative role has been referred for treatment after eight to twelve months of escalating difficulty completing a brief required weekly work presentation in front of an executive director and approximately ten managers. situation: The patient has spent the past eight months to a year feeling consumed by a weekly work presentation that lasts only a few minutes but dominates the entire week emotionally. At work, the patient sits in a circle with an executive director and about ten managers, waiting for a turn to give a short program update. By the night before, sleep is often impossible, and by the meeting itself there is intense physical panic: sweating, racing heart, red face, shaky hands, nausea, and a sense that everyone can see the distress. This pattern is not new: the patient has avoided public speaking since school. Overall, the patient seems trapped in a longstanding performance anxiety that now threatens both self-respect and career stability.

The new role brings several layers of anxiety at once: unfamiliar sales work, a draining commute, performance being judged more visibly, the possibility of failing to meet targets, and responsibility for subordinates whose results will also reflect on the patient. The patient seems especially distressed by the sense of being pushed into this role because someone else quit and a replacement was needed, while still feeling attached to the prior department. Practical concerns quickly turn into broader fears about stamina, adapting to a completely different kind of work, and having to lead people in an unfamiliar context. situation: The patient becomes anxious when speaking with people outside a close circle of friends and worries this will interfere with both present friendships and future workplace relationships. The core problem is not a lack of desire for connection but a sense that the mind goes blank unless the other person takes the lead, leaving the patient nervously waiting for someone else to start and silently hoping they keep the conversation going. Even when conversation does begin, the patient feels poor at back-and-forth exchange, tends to cut things short, and then feels guilty thinking the other person would have been happier with a better conversationalist. With friends, the anxiety fades once enough familiarity develops. But with people who are not yet friends, the patient's entire conversational repertoire seems to disappear, and even reasonable strategies such as asking about hobbies stall when the topic is unfamiliar. The patient admires people who are good conversationalists and judges themselves against them, yet also shows warmth, politeness, and a sincere wish to connect.

situation: The patient is a bank employee who for about six months has been living in fear of sudden episodes of racing heart, chest pain, breathlessness, and the conviction of dying. The first attack came on a hot day during a period of rising work stress after a new manager arrived and a new computer system increased pressure. The patient was so frightened that they sat down and called a family member for help. Since then the patient has become hyperaware of every heartbeat change, spiraling quickly into thoughts that the heart might stop, a fear intensified by a parent having died of a heart attack. Even though an ECG was normal, the patient still struggles to believe the heart is truly fine and only recently has begun to wonder whether panic could explain it. The patient now avoids going into town alone, depends on a partner for transport, has stopped exercising for fear of cardiac strain, and backed out of social plans imagining becoming ill and embarrassing everyone. The problem is shrinking daily life and straining an otherwise supportive relationship.

presenting_problem.situation: An adult man in manual work sought help as anxiety escalated in the lead-up to an employment exam for a civil-service career path he has been pursuing, with distress becoming more noticeable during unstructured time and beginning to affect physical wellbeing and day-to-day functioning.
impact: Persistent preoccupation with the upcoming employment exam across the day.
Difficulty disengaging from worry during periods of inactivity or quiet time.
Episodes of nausea and vomiting associated with increased anxiety.
Reduced concentration when trying to focus on everyday tasks.
Limited disclosure of symptom severity to friends despite visible distress.

precipitating_factors: The upcoming employment exam has become more immediate, increasing pressure around preparation and outcome.
The exam is linked to a hoped-for transition from manual work into a stable civil-service role, raising the personal and practical stakes of the event.

psychological: Age 11: after his parents separated, he remembers trying to keep worries to himself so as not to add pressure at home, especially when money was tight.
Late adolescence: he began taking on casual manual jobs early and learned that mistakes at work could lead to sharp criticism or lost shifts, making performance feel closely tied to security.
In his twenties: he developed a habit of mentally rehearsing worst-case outcomes before important tasks, telling himself this was how he stayed prepared.
social: He grew up in a working-class household where stable public-sector employment was spoken about as something to aim for because it meant steady pay, benefits, and less risk of sudden unemployment.

As a mixed-ethnicity man in manual work settings, he has often felt pressure to prove himself through reliability and not show distress openly, making it less likely that others notice when he is struggling.

internal: Unstructured time leads to worry about the exam, which increases physical arousal and makes the threat feel more immediate, leading to further worry.
Brief relief from distraction such as music or talking with friends reduces distress temporarily but does not change the underlying fear, so anxiety quickly returns once he is alone again.
Focus on possible negative outcomes interferes with concentration and recovery, which can then be interpreted as further evidence that he may not cope well with the exam.
external: The exam represents a high-stakes route to greater job security, keeping performance pressure constantly salient.
Because people around him do not fully see how severe the symptoms are, he may receive support that is comforting but insufficiently targeted to the level of impairment.

internal: He is strongly motivated by both personal ideals and practical career goals, which may support engagement with treatment.

external: He has friends he can talk to, and conversation with them provides temporary reduction in distress.
He remains employed, suggesting some ongoing daily structure and contact with others.
He has access to simple self-soothing routines such as listening to music that can interrupt escalation in the short term.

intermediate_beliefs: If I am not fully prepared and in control, I will mess it up and prove I'm not good enough.
Showing how badly I'm struggling will make people see me as weak or unreliable, so I need to keep it to myself.
The only way to stay safe is to think through every possible thing that could go wrong before it happens.

If I can't even settle myself down now, how am I supposed to cope when it really counts?
Don't let people see how bad this is or they'll think you're weak and useless.
triggers: Periods of quiet or unstructured time, especially when he is alone and his attention shifts back to the upcoming exam.
Reminders of the employment exam, preparation demands, or conversations about career stability and the consequences of failing.
In therapy, direct questions about how bad the symptoms really are, or encouragement to rely on support, can heighten his fear of being judged or seen as weak.
coping_patterns: He keeps busy with work, music, or conversation to block out worry, but seeks these distractions repeatedly when anxiety rises.
He limits how much he tells others about his symptoms, downplays the severity when asked, and tries to appear more in control than he feels.
He repeatedly rehearses possible problems, checks his readiness, and pushes himself to prepare longer even when physical distress is increasing.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: He appears more able to access anxiety, tension, irritability, and pressure than softer vulnerable states. He can feel fear strongly in his body, including nausea and agitation, but has more difficulty tolerating shame, sadness, disappointment, and dependence on others. Relief and steadiness are possible when he is distracted or occupied, though these states are hard for him to sustain during quiet or unstructured time.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants friends to notice that he is struggling, take him seriously, and offer support without making him feel exposed or judged.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he shows the full extent of his distress, friends will minimize it, tell him to just get on with it, or see him differently.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He hints at distress but withholds details, uses distraction and banter to keep interactions manageable, and then feels temporarily soothed but still alone with the problem.

interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He overprepares, monitors himself closely, pushes through physical distress, and becomes more tense and distracted when he fears he is slipping.

situation: The patient is increasingly preoccupied with an upcoming employment exam and finds that anxiety grows loudest whenever there is free time and nothing else occupying the mind. The patient repeatedly circles around questions such as whether the exam will be passed and what will happen otherwise, and the worry has become intense enough to cause physical symptoms including vomiting, even though friends do not know how severe the distress is. The career path seems emotionally important for both idealistic and practical reasons: the patient was inspired by seeing professionals in the field on television and values the stability of civil service. Even with these motivations, the patient seems easily pulled into overthinking and has trouble shifting out of fear when not actively engaged with something else. A few things help temporarily, such as talking with friends or listening to music, which suggests calm is possible when attention is redirected, but those strategies do not yet fully counter the underlying anxiety.

presenting_problem.situation: An early-adolescent girl was referred because of escalating school avoidance and distress since the transition to middle school, with worsening difficulty managing classroom attendance, peer interactions, and academic performance.
impact: Refuses or resists attending school and has wanted to go home upon arriving at class.
Becomes visibly distressed in the classroom, including hyperventilating and feeling physically sick when attention from peers is perceived.
Avoids approaching the homeroom teacher and has reduced participation in group-based classroom activities.
Shows marked difficulty concentrating in class and has had a decline in exam performance to below-average scores.
Spends free periods alone reading and remains socially isolated from classmates.

Recent increases in group assignments and free-form grouping have made her exclusion by peers more visible.
A noticeable drop in concentration and exam scores has brought school concerns to family or staff attention and increased pressure around attendance.

Shows marked difficulty concentrating in class and has had a decline in exam performance to below-average scores.
Spends free periods alone reading and remains socially isolated from classmates.
activation_tags: not having classmates to sit with

items.content: Heightened monitoring of classmates' facial expressions and whispering increases physical anxiety, which then makes staying in class harder and strengthens the urge to escape.
Avoiding school, group activities, or help-seeking brings short-term relief, but it increases isolation and makes returning to class feel more threatening the next time.

Falling concentration and lower exam scores create additional worry about being noticed negatively, which further intensifies anxiety in class; sadness appears secondary to this chronic exclusion and anxiety cycle.
activation_tags: worry about bad grades being noticed

items.content: Middle-school classes require frequent group work and informal peer grouping, repeatedly placing her in situations where she is left out or feels exposed.
Avoidance of the homeroom teacher reduces opportunities for adult support or correction of peer-related misunderstandings at school.

With peers/friends: Wish: She wants to be included, chosen, and allowed to belong without being embarrassed. | Expected response: She expects peers will overlook her, pair with others first, or make her exclusion visible if she tries to join. | Reaction: She becomes watchful and ashamed, stays on the edge of the group, avoids initiating, and retreats into solitary activities such as reading.
activation_tags: wanting to be chosen by peers
staying on the edge of the group

items.content: With parent/caregiver: Wish: She wants comfort, protection, and help managing school distress without feeling like a burden. | Expected response: She expects that if she shows how upset she is, a parent may become worried or distressed, which she experiences as something she should prevent. | Reaction: She withholds details, minimizes distress until it escalates, then may cling, resist school attendance, or seek proximity while struggling to explain what she needs.
activation_tags: wanting comfort without being a burden

situation: The patient does not want to go to school and has felt this way since starting middle school. The patient is intensely preoccupied with other people's eyes: when classmates look over and whisper, the assumption is they are saying bad things, and even when they avert their gaze the patient experiences it as being avoided. By the time the patient reaches the front of the classroom, turning around and going home feels overwhelmingly appealing. The patient has long been somewhat solitary, often reading alone at recess without minding too much, but middle school has made the pain sharper because group work and free-form grouping leave the patient visibly left out. Internally, the patient feels sad every day, believes everyone dislikes them, and becomes physically overwhelmed when dwelling on it, sometimes feeling sick or hyperventilating. Concentration has deteriorated badly and exam scores have fallen below average. At home the patient lives with family, likes one parent but worries that disclosing would only upset them, and has avoided the homeroom teacher.

demographics.name: Michael Turner
demographics.occupation: returning adult student; previously stay-at-home parent for approximately 20 years

presenting_problem.situation: An adult male returning student, previously a stay-at-home parent for approximately 20 years, sought treatment after seven to eight months of escalating anxiety following his return to school. Symptoms have begun to interfere with class attendance, concentration, academic performance, sleep, and evening coping routines, with increased concern after slipping grades and continued distress despite using alcohol and marijuana at night.
impact: Near-constant worry that shifts between school responsibilities and concerns about home
Difficulty sustaining attention in class and on schoolwork, with declining grades
Feeling persistently on edge with muscle tension, fatigue, and physical rigidity
Sleep disturbance marked by difficulty falling asleep, nightmares, and waking with racing thoughts
Nightly use of wine and marijuana in attempts to calm anxiety

precipitating_factors: Return to school after approximately 20 years as a stay-at-home parent
Recent academic feedback and slipping grades after expecting to perform at a very high level
Repeated transitions between being in class, being away from home, and anticipating the next school week

psychological: In late adolescence and early adulthood, he had a strong identity as a straight-A student and came to measure himself heavily through academic performance
For roughly 20 years of adulthood, he functioned primarily as the at-home parent, becoming accustomed to staying closely attuned to household needs and family routines
A grandparent had strongly encouraged his education, and that relationship gave school achievement lasting personal significance
social: For two decades, his daily role centered on caregiving and home management, leaving limited recent practice with academic demands and evaluation settings
As a returning adult student, he is re-entering an environment organized around deadlines, performance, and comparison after a long absence from formal education

internal: Worry about school and home reduces concentration, leading to poorer academic performance, which then creates more worry about school
Attempts to sleep are interrupted by physiological arousal and racing thoughts, and the resulting fatigue lowers coping capacity the next day, increasing anxiety
Using wine and marijuana at night provides short-term calming but does not resolve the anxiety, allowing the cycle of poor sleep, fatigue, and overwhelm to continue
external: Being away from home during class increases distraction and reinforces checking mentally on home matters rather than engaging with coursework
Ongoing academic demands, assignments, and receipt of grades provide repeated cues for renewed worry throughout the week and weekend

internal: Strong prior history of academic competence and persistence
Clear motivation to improve functioning in school and daily life
Able to identify current symptoms and report links between worry, sleep loss, and substance use
external: Has reached treatment while symptoms are causing impairment rather than fully withdrawing from school
Maintains an active role in family life and remains connected to home responsibilities
Is currently enrolled in school, providing access to structured routines and potential academic support resources

intermediate_beliefs: If I am not fully on top of school and home at all times, everything will start to fall apart and I will not be able to handle it.
I should be able to manage this on my own; if I need too much help, it means I am not coping.
If my performance slips, it means I am losing control and letting down what school has always meant about me and my life.
automatic_thoughts: I can't keep up with this, and if I fall behind any more I'm going to spiral.
If I'm this distracted in class, maybe I don't belong here anymore.
I should be able to handle school and home, but instead everything feels out of control.
triggers: Receiving grades, academic feedback, or noticing that his performance is slipping below his own expectations.
Preparing for class, sitting in class while away from home, or trying to shift attention from household concerns to coursework.
Nighttime attempts to fall asleep, weekend anticipation of the coming school week, and waking with racing thoughts about school and home.
coping_patterns: He overprepares for classes, repeatedly reviews assignments and grades, and spends long periods trying to get ahead, but then loses focus and becomes stuck or slows down when anxiety escalates.
He uses wine and marijuana at night to settle his body, stays up while trying to calm down, and enters the next day fatigued and less able to engage consistently with school demands.

He alternates between seeking reassurance from family about school and home matters and then pulling back, becoming quiet or less communicative when he feels too keyed up or ashamed about not coping well.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: He readily experiences worry, tension, guilt, discouragement, and mental/physical fatigue. He appears able to notice feeling overwhelmed and on edge. He has more difficulty staying with vulnerability-linked emotions such as helplessness, shame, and the wish to be supported, and he may move quickly into worry, overactivity, or evening substance use when those states intensify.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants his partner to recognize that he is struggling, provide steady reassurance, and help him feel supported without seeing him as incapable.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he shows too much anxiety or need, his partner will become worried, frustrated, or view him as less dependable.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He gives partial updates, asks for reassurance in moments of strain, and then retreats, becomes quiet, or minimizes the extent of his distress after feeling exposed.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants instructors to see him as capable, take his effort seriously, and allow room for him to regain his footing.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that signs of struggle will be read as evidence that he cannot keep up or does not belong in the academic setting anymore.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He monitors feedback closely, becomes tense and self-critical around grades, and may work harder in a pressured way while avoiding direct discussion of how impaired he has been feeling.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants help reducing his anxiety and improving functioning while feeling understood rather than judged for losing control or relying on alcohol and marijuana at night.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he reveals the full extent of his worry, impairment, or substance use, the therapist may judge him, push him too quickly, or see him as unable to cope.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He may initially present as cooperative and articulate but disclose selectively, test whether the therapist is steady, and shift between seeking guidance and holding back when sessions feel too exposing.

situation: The patient returned to school after 20 years as a stay-at-home parent once the children were grown, and for the past seven to eight months this transition has been overshadowed by relentless worry that feels present nearly all the time. During the week the patient worries about school, but in class cannot stay mentally present because of preoccupation with what might be happening at home; on weekends the worry shifts back to school starting again. The patient expected to resume school as the straight-A student they once were, but grades are slipping because worry crowds out focus. The patient describes feeling constantly on edge, tired, tense, and rigid, and sleep has become a cycle of struggling to fall asleep, waking from nightmares, and jolting awake with racing thoughts. There is also an emotional burden tied to a grandparent who had strongly encouraged the patient's education; doing poorly now feels like a betrayal of that memory. To settle nerves the patient has been drinking wine at night and using marijuana, but still feels overwhelmed.

presenting_problem.situation: An adult male student on professional placement was referred for treatment after increasing difficulty in client-facing interactions became apparent during training activities and role-play exercises, with anxiety-related behaviors interfering with his communication and confidence in placement-based social performance.
impact: Marked reduction in eye contact during client-facing conversations on placement.
Grips objects tightly and visibly tenses muscles while speaking with clients or in role-play tasks.
Selects layered clothing or all-black outfits to reduce visibility of sweating during placement days.
Communication becomes hesitant and less fluid in work-related social interactions, particularly when speaking to clients.
Avoids or limits participation in situations that require direct client interaction or being closely observed.

precipitating_factors: Transition into a professional placement with regular client-facing responsibilities and observed communication tasks.
Recent role-play and performance-based training exercises made the difficulties more visible to supervisors and training staff.
Increased frequency of speaking directly with clients raised the practical impact of the problem on placement performance and prompted referral.

psychological: Age 13: during a classroom presentation at secondary school, he became flushed, stumbled over his words, and noticed several classmates laughing afterward.
A repeated adolescent pattern of avoiding putting his hand up in class unless he was certain of the answer, especially in subjects where peers were outspoken or critical.

First year of university: after being asked to introduce himself in a seminar, he spoke briefly, looked down for most of the time, and then avoided speaking in later sessions unless directly called on.
social: Grew up in school and peer settings where confidence, quick verbal responses, and not showing nervousness were treated as markers of competence for boys and young men.
Entered a competitive training environment in which presentations, observed practice, and peer comparison are routine, making visible signs of nervousness feel especially consequential.

internal: Anticipation of visible anxiety leads him to avoid eye contact, grip objects, and tense his muscles; these behaviors narrow attention onto bodily sensations and make speaking less natural, which then increases concern about how he appears.

Wearing extra layers and choosing dark clothing reduces immediate discomfort about sweating, reinforcing the idea that visible signs must be concealed and increasing reliance on these behaviors in future interactions.

After social-performance situations, he continues to overestimate how noticeable shaking, redness, and sweating were, which strengthens anxiety before the next client encounter and increases use of protective behaviors.
external: Client-facing placement tasks repeatedly place him in situations where he feels closely observed and evaluated.
Professional training settings emphasize performance, observation, and feedback, increasing self-focused attention during interactions.

internal: Willing to attend treatment and take part in behavioral exercises.
Able to reflect on feedback and compare predictions with observed outcomes.
Shows emerging capacity to revise assumptions after video review demonstrated less visible anxiety than expected.
external: Enrolled in a structured training placement with access to supervision and skills-based feedback.
Has opportunity for graded practice through role-play and observed placement tasks.
Remains engaged in education and professional training, preserving daily structure and future goals.

intermediate_beliefs: If I cannot keep my anxiety hidden when speaking to clients, people will see that I am not able to cope.
I need to stay tightly controlled and avoid drawing attention, or I will lose control and get stuck in the interaction.
It is safer to say less, look away, and prepare carefully than to risk showing nerves and being judged.
automatic_thoughts: They can see I'm anxious and I'm losing it.
If I mess this up, they'll see I can't cope in front of clients.
I need to get through this without showing anything.
triggers: Observed client-facing conversations, role-plays, or presentations where he may be watched and evaluated.
Moments when he notices bodily signs such as sweating, facial warmth, shaking, or muscle tension while speaking.
In therapy, being asked to do an in-session role-play, review video feedback, or speak at length while the therapist closely observes him.
coping_patterns: Avoids or limits participation in situations requiring direct client interaction or close observation.
Reduces eye contact, gives short or hesitant responses, and stays in the background during role-plays or group discussions.
Wears layered or dark clothing, grips objects tightly, and holds his body rigid during client-facing interactions.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: He readily experiences anxiety, embarrassment, apprehension, and shame in evaluative social situations. He can access determination and relief after practice goes better than expected, but finds it harder to tolerate visible vulnerability, open self-consciousness, and sustained expressions of need or helplessness in front of others.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants the therapist to be calm, respectful, and to help him improve without making him feel exposed or foolish.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if his anxiety becomes visible in session or during behavioral exercises, the therapist may notice his awkwardness, focus on his performance, and view him as less capable than he should be.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He becomes quieter, reduces eye contact, gives brief answers, watches the therapist closely for signs of evaluation, and participates more cautiously in role-play or feedback tasks.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants supervisors to see him as competent, professional, and improving in client-facing work.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that visible nervousness, hesitant speech, or sweating will be taken as evidence that he cannot manage client interactions confidently enough for placement demands.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He speaks less fluently, grips objects, tenses his body, limits spontaneous contributions, and avoids or minimizes opportunities for direct client-facing practice when possible.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants peers to treat him as capable and not single him out for nervousness during observed tasks or role-plays.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that peers will notice signs of anxiety, compare him unfavorably, or remember moments where he appeared shaky or unsure.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He stays in the background during group exercises, avoids volunteering first, keeps conversation brief, and uses clothing choices and reduced eye contact to draw less attention to himself.

situation: The patient becomes intensely self-conscious in work-related social situations, especially when speaking with clients, and carries a vivid mental image of being obviously anxious, out of place, red-faced, visibly shaking, sweating, and unable to communicate properly. The fear is not just about feeling anxious but about others being able to see it and judging accordingly. To manage this, the patient grips tightly onto whatever is in hand, clenches muscles, avoids eye contact, and wears layers or all black so sweating will be less noticeable. The patient believes these protective habits keep things from becoming worse and expects that dropping them would lead to more shaking and foolishness. However, in a role-play exercise, the patient predicted extreme shaking, redness, and sweating, yet when watching themselves on video was surprised to see far less than expected and appeared more natural and personable without the safety behaviors. The patient still overestimates how obvious the anxiety is but is beginning to see that internal experience and outward appearance are not the same.

presenting_problem.situation: Referred by a school counselor after several months of noticeable social withdrawal, reduced lunch intake, and a decline in engagement despite continued school attendance and adequate assignment completion. Concern increased when teachers observed that she appeared persistently tired, detached from peers, and difficult to draw into conversation.
impact: Spends most non-school time isolated in her room and has reduced contact with friends.
Frequently skips meals or eats very little at school and at home.
Appears persistently sad, flat, and low in energy.
Reports difficulty concentrating and is completing schoolwork in a mechanical, minimally engaged way.
Has decreased participation in previously typical social and school-related activities.

precipitating_factors: Over the past school term, the parent’s work demands appear to have increased, with less time at home and greater visible financial stress.
As peer activities and school expenses increased during the school year, she further reduced social participation and stopped raising routine needs at home.
Teachers and the school counselor became more concerned after observing persistent withdrawal, low energy, and reduced eating over several months.

psychological: Age 12: after her parent took on additional shifts, she began spending more afternoons and evenings alone at home and started handling her own meals and school preparation without asking for help.

Age 13: she stopped mentioning routine school needs such as field trip fees, supplies, and replacement clothing after seeing her parent become visibly stressed while reviewing bills at the kitchen table.
Over the past 1-2 years, she has developed a pattern of withdrawing to her room when upset and keeping problems to herself rather than seeking comfort or assistance.
social: Since early adolescence, she has lived with a single parent who works multiple jobs, leaving the household organized around scarcity, exhaustion, and trying not to add demands.

In her school and home life, limited money for food, clothes, activities, and supplies has repeatedly signaled that needs must be deferred, and she has had fewer chances for low-cost social participation with peers.

internal: Avoids asking for food, supplies, or help -> immediate relief from feeling demanding -> needs go unmet -> physical depletion and low mood worsen.
Withdraws to her room and reduces social contact -> temporary escape from effort and expense -> increased isolation -> sadness and detachment deepen.
Completes school tasks by going through the motions without seeking support -> performance stays superficially adequate -> distress is underestimated by others -> the pattern continues.
external: The parent’s long work hours and financial strain leave little time and emotional space for problems to be discussed, so symptoms remain largely unseen at home.
Limited household money makes ordinary adolescent activities, school extras, and shared outings harder to access, reinforcing withdrawal from peers.

internal: Able to describe routines and recent changes in mood and behavior when asked directly.
Shows conscientiousness and a strong sense of responsibility toward family obligations.
Retains some investment in school and future stability despite low motivation.
external: Ongoing attachment to her parent and a wish to protect that relationship.
School access to a counselor and observing adults who have already noticed the change in functioning.
Continues to attend school regularly and maintains basic academic responsibilities.

intermediate_beliefs: If I need too much, people will get stressed out or pull away, so I should handle things on my own.
It is better to go without than to make trouble or cost my parent more money.
If I act like I am fine and keep up at school, nobody will be disappointed in me or see me as a problem.
automatic_thoughts: I should just deal with it myself.
If I say I need something, I'll just make things worse.
Nobody's really going to want to hear all of this.
triggers: Situations where she has to ask for money, food, school supplies, fees, or help at home or school.
Seeing her parent tired, worried about bills, rushing between jobs, or reacting with visible stress to expenses.
In therapy or at school, being asked direct questions about sadness, eating, loneliness, or whether things are hard at home.
coping_patterns: Keeps distress private, gives brief minimal answers when adults ask how she is doing, and downplays problems until others notice changes in eating, energy, or participation.
Withdraws to her room after school, reduces texting and time with friends, and stops joining optional school or peer activities when she feels low or burdensome.
Continues attending school and completing assignments in a mechanical, conscientious way while avoiding requests for help, supplies, food, or accommodations.
psychological_formulation.emotional_range: She more readily accesses tiredness, numbness, guilt, embarrassment, and quiet sadness than overt anger or direct expressions of need. Longing for comfort and fear of being unwanted appear present but are difficult for her to tolerate or show openly, so vulnerable feelings are often flattened, hidden, or converted into withdrawal.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: She wants care, reassurance, and practical help while still feeling close to her parent.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: She expects that if she brings up needs, her parent will become more stressed, overwhelmed, or unavailable because of work and money pressures.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: She feels guilty and lonely, minimizes her needs, avoids asking for food, supplies, or comfort, and tries to appear self-sufficient.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: She wants inclusion, easy companionship, and to feel wanted without having to explain much.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: She expects that if she cannot keep up socially, seems down, or needs understanding, peers will lose interest, not notice, or see her as awkward and different.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: She becomes quiet and detached, declines invitations, communicates less, and waits for others to make contact while acting as though she does not mind.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: She wants a calm, steady adult who notices her distress and understands without pressuring or judging her.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: She expects that if she shows too much sadness, need, or family strain, the therapist may pity her, push her to talk before she is ready, or see her as overreacting.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: She initially stays guarded, gives sparse factual answers, watches closely for signs of judgment or pressure, and may comply on the surface without fully sharing more painful material.

situation: The patient is a teenager living with a single parent who works multiple jobs to keep the household afloat, and has gradually come to believe that simply existing and having needs makes the parent's already difficult life harder. The patient describes feeling guilty about everything from eating food in the house to asking for school supplies, and tries to take up as little space as possible by staying in their room, skipping meals, and never mentioning when something is needed. At school the patient functions adequately but feels detached and heavy, as though going through the motions without any sense that efforts matter. Friendships have been dropped because socializing requires energy and sometimes money the patient does not want to ask for, and the isolation has deepened a persistent sadness. situation: The patient comes in describing poor sleep, dark thoughts, emotional numbness alternating with unexplained crying, and a bleak, almost philosophical hopelessness in which everything feels meaningless and like a distraction from mortality. The patient says it is not exactly a wish to die, but that there are times of not wanting to live, suggesting a heavy kind of despair rather than a simple complaint about low mood. What stands out is how exposed and defensive the patient becomes when trying to talk about it: there seems to be a reaching for help, possibly even considering medication, but the patient quickly feels misunderstood and accused when the response does not match the seriousness of the inner state. The result is that sadness and overwhelm rapidly turn into irritation, distrust, and withdrawal. Even in a brief exchange, the patient comes across as someone who has been carrying a lot alone and who is frightened enough by their own thoughts to finally speak, while also being highly sensitive to feeling mocked or not believed.

presenting_problem.situation: An adult male manual worker was referred for assessment after several months of persistent low mood and anxiety following news that a parent with cancer is expected to have limited time left. Help is being sought now in the context of continued distress, sleep disruption, and reduced concentration while he is also living apart from his spouse and managing family responsibilities largely on his own.

Next-day tiredness while continuing manual work responsibilities.
Reduced concentration during child-related tasks and other daily responsibilities.
Mood lift from seeing friends is short-lived, with distress returning afterward.

precipitating_factors: Learning that his parent has cancer with an estimated prognosis of about 18 months.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants reassurance, practical sharing of the load, and to feel understood without having to spell out too much vulnerability.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he shows how overwhelmed or needy he feels, his partner may feel burdened, too far away to really help, or may respond in ways that leave him feeling more alone.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He minimizes distress in contact, sticks to practical updates, and tries to carry on independently while feeling privately resentful, flat, or unsupported.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants companionship, brief relief, and a sense of normality without having to expose too much of what is going on emotionally.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_other: He expects that if he goes beyond surface-level sharing, others may not know what to say, may offer clichés, or may see him as not coping.
interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He agrees to social contact and can seem lighter for a short time, but keeps conversations on safer topics, leaves without having processed much, and returns to managing distress on his own afterward.

interpersonal_patterns.wish: He wants practical help to steady his sleep, concentration, and mood, while also wanting to feel respected rather than pitied.

interpersonal_patterns.response_of_self: He presents as controlled and cooperative, emphasizes facts over feelings, tests whether the therapist is useful and non-intrusive, and may downplay the intensity of distress unless trust builds gradually.

situation: The patient has been feeling persistently low and anxious since learning that a parent with cancer likely has only about a year and a half left to live. The emotional burden is complicated by living apart from a spouse who is in another country, so although they can still meet online and support one another, the patient experiences much of the situation as an isolated struggle. What seems to trouble the patient most is not day-to-day caregiving but the knowledge that time with the parent is limited and that a future without them is now real and approaching. When free time arrives, the mind starts racing with overthinking, becoming anxious not only about loss and sadness but about whether the current state could spiral into something worse. The patient also mentions feeling as if fighting a lone battle with a child's matters as well, adding to the sense that there is always something to carry. Although the patient can name temporary reliefs such as socializing with friends, these only lift the mood briefly.

presenting_problem.situation: A 74-year-old Caucasian woman who lives alone and works part-time in a service role was referred for assessment after three months of marked decline in daily functioning following the death of her long-term pet. Since the loss, her routine, self-care, social contact, and work functioning have deteriorated, raising concern for a depressive episode in addition to bereavement; medical, substance-related, and bipolar contributors are to be assessed.
impact: Frequent crying spells observed and reported across the day.
Marked loss of interest in meals, exercise, and previously maintained social contact.
Reduced appetite with irregular eating.
Difficulty maintaining household tasks and daily routine in the apartment.
Subjective difficulty concentrating, with slowed completion of chores and trouble staying focused during work tasks.

precipitating_factors: Death of her pet three months ago after fourteen years of providing daily companionship and routine.
Progressive loss of daily structure since the pet's death, including stopping morning walks, irregular meals, and reduced contact with friends.
Recent disclosure during a routine primary care visit after visible tearfulness and report of declining ability to manage usual self-care and part-time service work responsibilities.

psychological: Age 11: after her parents' divorce, she spent many afternoons alone until her mother returned from work, learning to keep distress private and rely on routines to get through the day.
Age 39: following the death of her husband, she returned to work within two weeks and managed grief largely by staying busy and avoiding discussion of the loss.
Around age 67: after reducing to part-time service work, most evenings were spent at home with the pet, and the animal became her main source of comfort and daily purpose.
social: For years in her social circle and workplace, she heard the message that 'you just keep going' and do not burden others with private upset, especially after losses that others may see as minor.

She lives alone in an apartment with limited nearby family contact, and several friendships narrowed after retirement-age transitions and schedule changes, leaving the pet as her most consistent companion.

Withdrawal from walks, meals, and social contact reduces activity and reinforcement, which worsens low mood and further decreases motivation.
Shame about the intensity of her grief leads her to hide symptoms, limiting support and delaying corrective feedback or help-seeking.
external: The apartment contains the pet's belongings in their usual places, creating repeated cues for grief and making routine reorganization less likely.
Comments from others to 'get another animal' or move on have reduced fuller disclosure and increased isolation from available support.

She was willing to describe the recent decline when asked directly in medical care.
She appears capable of forming strong attachment and caring routines, which can be redirected into treatment goals.
external: She remains connected to a primary care clinician who identified the decline and facilitated referral.
A small group of friends continues to check in and offer practical contact, even if their responses have not always felt helpful.
She has stable housing and an ongoing part-time job that provides some external structure.
